report:
### Conclusion
The claim that conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) supplements meaningfully reduce abdominal fat in humans is poorly supported by current scientific evidence. 

### Key Evidence
* **Animal vs. Human Results:** CLA demonstrated significant body fat reduction in animal studies, but these effects have largely failed to replicate in human clinical trials.
* **Small Early Studies:** A few small, early randomized trials found minor reductions in abdominal adipose tissue in specific subgroups, such as abdominally obese men ([Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/0801659)).
* **Systematic Reviews & Meta-Analyses:** Broader human evidence indicates that CLA's effect on fat loss is negligible. A meta-analysis in *The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* found an average fat loss of only ~0.05 kg (0.1 lbs) per week ([AJCN](https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)28055-7/fulltext)). A 2023 systematic review in the *British Journal of Nutrition* similarly concluded that high-quality human trials fail to demonstrate meaningful body fat-lowering properties ([British Journal of Nutrition](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-doseresponse-metaanalysis/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366)).
* **Metabolic Safety Concerns:** Research cautions that long-term supplementation with certain CLA isomers may adversely affect metabolic health, including worsening insulin sensitivity or increasing liver fat ([Healthline](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/conjugated-linoleic-acid)).

Overall, CLA supplementation does not produce clinically meaningful abdominal fat loss in humans.
